metadata.title: End-to-End Production Capstone Project
metadata.topics: Full production multi-agent platform (FastAPI, PostgreSQL/pgvector, MongoDB, Redis, MCP, A2A, Docker, K8s, Prometheus, Grafana, OTel) — monorepo build & verification

sections.mental-model:
A production agent platform is a durable application that delegates a few decisions to a model. Its hardest problem is recovering partial work without losing the user's request, inventing evidence, exposing another tenant's data, or repeating an effect. Treat an agent's output as a proposal that crosses a typed and authorized boundary, then let application state decide what happens next.

Picture a public library policy desk. The intake clerk accepts a question and issues a receipt. A research librarian finds the applicable edition of a policy and records page numbers. A second librarian checks that the policy supports the answer. A supervisor controls anything that leaves the staff workflow. Each person can walk away mid-shift because the receipt, evidence, and decision are written down. Redis can call the next ticket number, PostgreSQL owns the ticket record, and nobody gives the research librarian access to payroll because they can read a policy.

### Turn the analogy into invariants

- **Durable receipt.** After the API says a task was accepted, either its result becomes available or its terminal failure is recorded. If queue publication fails, the task remains discoverable from durable state.
- **Recoverable execution.** A worker can disappear between any two steps. Starting another attempt neither reopens a finished task nor loses a committed result. If a future integration sends an external notification, retries carry a stable operation ID and reconcile uncertain outcomes.
- **Tenant boundary.** Identity, tenant, and allowed capabilities come from authenticated application context. The model supplies subject matter. Every data access and delegation checks scope again at the destination.
- **Grounded output.** Each material claim refers to a source in the authorized evidence set, down to the document revision and chunk. The answer can say evidence is missing. Fluency carries no authority.
- **Finite work.** Every task has a deadline, attempt budget, token budget, and cap on tool steps. A retry consumes those same budgets. A queued task that can no longer meet its deadline enters a visible terminal state.
- **Inspectable operations.** The operator can distinguish queue delay, retrieval delay, and excessive generation. Their dashboards contain timings and counts. Prompt text, document contents, and raw identifiers stay out of metrics.

### Start with one vertical slice

Build one path from an accepted question to a cited answer using a deterministic fixture model. Add the queue and crash recovery before introducing model randomness. Add a narrowly scoped retrieval MCP service once the local contract works. Split independent verification behind A2A only after the workflow benefits from separate ownership or deployment. The running system should still be testable with a fixture model and fixture agent after the realistic integrations arrive.

A monorepo can hold independently deployable services while a common package shares versioned contracts. Keep FastAPI for request handling and status polling, execution in a worker, and one service for each boundary that needs different access or independent scale. Do not split simple functions into deployments just to maximize the service count. Local Compose should make the happy path reproducible. A Kubernetes deployment should help you prove resource limits, safe rollout, and recovery under failure.
sections.architecture:
The capstone lab follows a **Public Library Policy Desk**. Staff submit a question about circulation, room booking, or accessibility. The result cites one or more approved policy passages and marks any unsupported portion as unresolved. Treat the model and all retrieved text as untrusted input. The workflow can read approved material and publish a reply into the same task record.

```text
 [Staff UI] --- HTTPS POST /tasks; GET /tasks/{id} ---> [FastAPI]
                                                         |
                                    accept transaction    | task + outbox
                                                         v
                                             [PostgreSQL + pgvector]
                                                         ^
                                                         | task transitions
                         [Outbox relay]                  | checkpoints/results
                               | XADD                    |
                               v                         |
                       [Redis Stream] -- claim ------> [Worker / orchestrator]
                                                         |          |
                              MCP: list/call authorized |          | A2A: verify
                                      read-only tool    |          | task lifecycle
                                                         v          v
                                               [Policy search]  [Verifier service]
                                                         |
                                  tenant + corpus filter | lexical + vector search
                                                         v
                                              [PostgreSQL + pgvector]

 [Worker / API / services] --- scoped events ------> [MongoDB trajectories]
 [API / worker / tools] ------- OTLP ---------------> [Collector]
                                                            |
                                         metrics ----------> [Prometheus -> Grafana]
                                         traces/logs ------> [Configured backends]
```

### Choose what survives each failure

| Component | Owns | Recovery implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FastAPI | Authentication, validation, request acceptance, task status | Replica shutdown can lose a connection. The client can safely retry acceptance with the same key. |
| PostgreSQL | Tasks, leases, canonical checkpoints/results, idempotency records, outbox, dataset metadata | It is the authority when the queue, a cache, and a worker disagree. |
| PostgreSQL + pgvector | Authorized policy revisions, chunks, lexical text indexes, and embeddings | Rebuild embeddings from a versioned corpus. Pin an accepted task to one revision set so citations remain reproducible. |
| MongoDB | Flexible, redacted trajectory events keyed by task, attempt, and sequence | Repeated telemetry delivery can upsert the same event. Query the protected store for investigation. Agent completion state remains in PostgreSQL. |
| Redis | Work notification through Streams, short-lived rate-limit counters and cache | Unacknowledged stream entries can be reclaimed. An outbox or reconciliation loop can reissue notifications when Redis loses volatile data. |
| MCP | Callable access to policy retrieval through a defined tool schema | Return structured evidence IDs and text. The server checks permissions and enforces the query limit. |
| A2A | An independent verifier's capability and task lifecycle | Persist the provider task identifier as soon as it is known. Use its status/results to resume instead of issuing a new task at every poll. |

### From request to result

1. **Accept durably.** Resolve identity and tenant, validate an idempotency key, and hash a canonical form of the request payload. In one database transaction write the task and its outbox record. Use a uniqueness constraint on tenant and operation key. The API returns HTTP 202 with the task identifier and status URL after commit. A request with the same tenant, key, and payload returns the existing receipt. A different payload reusing that key gets a conflict. Scope status lookup by tenant even if task IDs are unguessable.
2. **Deliver at least once.** The relay reads unsent outbox rows, publishes task IDs into the stream, and records delivery. It can crash after publication and before recording delivery, so duplicates are normal. A consumer group assigns entries to workers and tracks pending deliveries. A task claim checks durable state, assigns a lease with a monotonic generation number, and commits before the worker does expensive I/O. A worker whose generation no longer matches cannot overwrite a newer attempt. Keep leases short enough for recovery, renew them during legitimate slow work, and use a separate hard deadline for task lifetime. Acknowledge the stream after a terminal checkpoint or a durable retry handoff. Expired leases and old pending entries require reconciliation.
3. **Publish a consistent corpus.** Ingestion stores the policy revision, extracted text, document ownership, chunk offsets, embedding model version, and a stable evidence ID. Stage an updated revision, check row counts and search quality, then atomically mark it available. Pin accepted work to that published revision. Keep retired chunks through the citation retention period. A stale cache entry cannot turn an obsolete revision into the applicable policy.
4. **Retrieve bounded evidence.** First constrain candidates by tenant and pinned corpus revision. Run lexical and vector searches within that scope. Lexical search catches exact terms such as “temporary resident card” and identifiers. Embeddings can recognize “someone living here for the summer” even when the phrasing differs. Fuse rank lists and cap what goes into the context window. For approximate vector indexes, selective filters can leave fewer results than expected. Measure against an exact scan on a sample, track short result sets, and fall back to exact search over a small filtered partition where justified. Recheck authorization when loading the chosen chunks, including from cache.
5. **Delegate precisely.** The model can propose a retrieval query and structured answer. It cannot create tools, choose an arbitrary remote endpoint, or pass tenant identity as an authority. The worker calls a known MCP tool using its schema, service credentials, and a limited deadline. MCP exposes tools that can be invoked, resources the client can read, and prompts the client can use as templates. Here one tool suffices. The separate A2A verifier advertises a verification skill in an Agent Card. Configure the peer endpoint and trust relationship. Send only the minimal answer and authorized evidence identifiers or policy excerpts the verifier needs. Check the capability version, allowed audience, verifier output schema, and remote task state. Keep the workflow capable of ending with a clear incomplete result if the verifier is unavailable.
6. **Commit the terminal outcome.** Validate claim-to-evidence links and confirm that the verifying response matches the intended answer and corpus. In one short transaction, check the lease generation and persist the terminal state and reply. Treat old attempts' later responses as stale. If the response is committed and the worker dies before queue acknowledgement, a successor sees the terminal state, skips execution, and acknowledges the duplicate. Status polling reads that durable result.
7. **Record evidence of behavior.** Emit one trace for the acceptance path and link it to the asynchronous worker trace. Capture queue wait, attempt number, stage latency, aggregate token use, retrieval result count, and delegated status. Use normal span links for work that starts later or joins multiple producers. A trace is diagnostic evidence, while task state is the recoverable application record.

### Retry, cancellation, and approval

Set a total deadline at acceptance, then derive bounded timeouts for individual dependencies from the remaining budget. Retry transient failures only when the action is known to be repeatable or supported by idempotency. Exponential backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retries. A stalled dependency needs a budget and a circuit breaker. Carry a small bounded cutoff for queue age so increasing retries cannot keep hopeless work alive.

Keep cancellation durable. A cancellation request can stop future steps and request cancellation of remote work. Already committed effects stay committed. Check for cancellation before claiming work, before delegation, and in the conditional final update. A remote result arriving after cancellation should be recorded or discarded according to policy without advancing the local task.

The lab has no authority to send a message outside the task. If an approved extension proposes sending a policy update to subscribers, persist the vetted effect payload, hash, approver identity, expiry, and target before release. Approval binds to the exact action, audience, and payload. Any change needs a new decision. A payload signed off yesterday does not imply approval for a materially different action today. If the provider has no idempotency contract, a timeout after submission requires reconciliation or operator review before retrying.
sections.syntax:
### Validate a boundary before invoking a tool

A strict Pydantic schema gives the research tool a usable contract and a finite result limit. Define the authority separately so it cannot be accepted as an incidental argument.

```python
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class SearchPolicy(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)
    query: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=400)]
    limit: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=10)] = 5


parsed = SearchPolicy.model_validate({"query": "room reservation", "limit": 3})
print(parsed.limit)
```

The script prints `3`. `extra="forbid"` refuses unrecognized fields, including an injected `tenant_id`. `strict=True` does not coerce strings such as `"3"` into integers. `Annotated` retains the type and gives Pydantic validated field limits. `model_validate` accepts a value and returns a validated `SearchPolicy` or raises a validation error. Apply equivalent validation to the returned evidence before adding it to context. Send validation failures as structured errors, and limit how often the model may correct invalid arguments.

### Combine search ranks without mixing score scales

Cosine distance and text ranking scores use different scales. Reciprocal rank fusion adds values of the form `1 / (k + rank)` from each ordered list, using ranks starting at one. A missing item contributes zero for that list. Starting with a relatively small `k` such as 20 for an experiment gives top positions more influence than a very large `k`. Pick the settings on judged data.

Suppose exact search ranks policy A first and B second. Semantic search ranks policy C first and B second. A and C each get about 0.0476 from a single first place. B gets about 0.0909 across two second places. When agreement helps, B should move first. The example also shows a limitation. If the request contains an authoritative policy number, one exceptional exact match may deserve special treatment even if only one searcher found it. Apply a deterministic exact identifier rule or measure a separately weighted fusion variant.

### Commit only the worker that still owns the attempt

A lease is an agreement with an expiry. Its generation protects against a worker that resumes after a replacement has already taken over. The following update is shown for a parameterized psycopg call. Bind `task`, `tenant`, `generation`, and `answer` from trusted application data.

```sql
UPDATE tasks
SET state = 'succeeded', answer = %(answer)s, lease_expires_at = NULL
WHERE id = %(task)s
  AND tenant_id = %(tenant)s
  AND state = 'running'
  AND lease_generation = %(generation)s
  AND lease_expires_at > CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
RETURNING id;
```

`SET` records the reply and closes the lease in the same row update. The predicates restrict the write to the current tenant, active attempt, generation, and deadline. On the winning attempt, `RETURNING id` yields one row. A concurrent cancellation, expired lease, or newer generation yields zero rows. Drop the stale result and re-read durable state in that case. Keep the commit transaction short. PostgreSQL's `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` is fixed at transaction start, so do not open this transaction before a long network call. Store the delivery acknowledgement after the commit. If lineage or a separate result table is required, update those rows in the same transaction.

### Read the rollout and the latency signal

```bash
kubectl rollout status deployment/policy-api --namespace policy-desk --timeout=90s
```

`rollout status` watches deployment progress. `deployment/policy-api` identifies the API deployment, `--namespace policy-desk` selects the namespace, and `--timeout=90s` caps how long the command waits. A successful check prints that the deployment rolled out. That means the readiness criteria and replica availability were met. Follow with a functional request that returns a cited result from a known authorized fixture.

For a histogram named `agent_task_duration_seconds`, an aggregate p95 over completed tasks can be expressed as follows.

```promql
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(agent_task_duration_seconds_bucket[10m])))
```

`_bucket` is the cumulative bucket series from a classic Prometheus histogram. `rate(...[10m])` computes per-second growth over ten minutes and handles counter resets. Summing by `le` combines replicas while retaining the upper bound for each bucket. `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` estimates the latency at the 95th percentile from bucket counts. The result is in seconds because the observations use seconds. Keep the same bucket boundaries across service replicas. An empty or sparse window may not supply a useful value. Inspect count and error rate alongside it, and separate queue wait from active execution with another histogram.
sections.lab:
### Repository blueprint for the library policy desk

Keep the deployable services in one repository, using explicit contracts rather than cross-imports between applications.

```text
policy-desk/
  apps/
    api/                  # FastAPI intake and owner-scoped status
    worker/               # task transitions, budgets, retrieval client
    policy_search/        # MCP read-only search against scoped pgvector
    verification_peer/    # A2A claim and evidence checks
  packages/
    contracts/            # request, result, event, and evidence schemas
    policy_core/          # deterministic authorization and validation
  migrations/postgres/    # task, outbox, corpus, index migrations
  deploy/
    compose/              # local services and synthetic fixtures
    k8s/                  # API, worker, relay, collector, and network policy
  observability/
    dashboards/           # workflow, dependencies, and quality panels
    alerts/               # queue age, errors, and budget alerts
  tests/
    contract/             # MCP and A2A input and output versions
    integration/          # stream, database, and peer failure scenarios
    evals/                # fixture prompts and evidence assertions
  labs/
    policy_slice.py       # local crash-and-resume exercise
```

### Run the narrow recovery slice

The example below isolates the critical commit/ack transition with SQLite and an in-process notification. It deliberately uses deterministic evidence so there is a precise expected answer. In the full platform, PostgreSQL owns this state, a transactional outbox publishes notifications, Redis delivers them, and a verifier checks the structured answer before it can be stored.

Save the example as `policy_slice.py`. Run `python3 policy_slice.py` with Python 3.12 or newer. `python3` starts the interpreter and the file argument chooses the entry point. No services or credentials are required.

```python
from contextlib import closing
from pathlib import Path
import sqlite3
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory


def deliver(db: sqlite3.Connection, tenant: str, task: str) -> str:
    row = db.execute(
        "SELECT state, reply FROM tasks WHERE tenant = ? AND id = ?",
        (tenant, task),
    ).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        raise LookupError("Task is unavailable in this scope")
    state, existing_reply = row
    if state == "succeeded":
        return existing_reply

    # The fixture stands in for scoped retrieval and verification.
    reply = "Book in person up to 14 days ahead. [rooms:v3:4]"
    with db:
        db.execute(
            "UPDATE tasks SET state = 'succeeded', reply = ? "
            "WHERE tenant = ? AND id = ? AND state = 'queued'",
            (reply, tenant, task),
        )
    stored = db.execute(
        "SELECT reply FROM tasks WHERE tenant = ? AND id = ?",
        (tenant, task),
    ).fetchone()
    return stored[0]


with TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    path = Path(temp_dir) / "tasks.sqlite"
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as db:
        with db:
            db.execute(
                "CREATE TABLE tasks (tenant TEXT, id TEXT, state TEXT, reply TEXT, "
                "PRIMARY KEY (tenant, id))"
            )
            db.execute(
                "INSERT INTO tasks VALUES (?, ?, 'queued', NULL)",
                ("library-a", "task-1"),
            )
        print("first delivery:", deliver(db, "library-a", "task-1"))
        # Pretend the worker stops after committing, before acknowledging.

    # A new connection represents a successor worker on redelivery.
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as db:
        print("second delivery:", deliver(db, "library-a", "task-1"))
        try:
            deliver(db, "library-b", "task-1")
        except LookupError:
            print("different tenant: denied")
```

Expected output:

```text
first delivery: Book in person up to 14 days ahead. [rooms:v3:4]
second delivery: Book in person up to 14 days ahead. [rooms:v3:4]
different tenant: denied
```

SQLite `execute` binds each question-mark placeholder from the tuple in order. The composite primary key makes the task identifier unique within its tenant. `fetchone` returns a row tuple or `None`. The transaction context commits statements in the block on success and rolls them back on an exception. `closing` closes each connection separately. `TemporaryDirectory` keeps the same database across connections, then cleans it up. The first delivery switches state conditionally, then the second delivery returns the stored reply. The fixture intentionally skips parallel claims. Use the lease and unique-key patterns for concurrent worker tests in the full build.

### Walk the same request through the full stack

Use synthetic policies for two library systems. For Library A, publish a policy revision that allows reservations in person up to 14 days ahead. Add an obsolete revision that says 30 days and a Library B revision that says 21 days. Seed all of them into the database and indexes so a test can detect accidentally dropping either filter. Add a second Library A clause about accessibility accommodations. Ask “How early may I book a room in person, and is there a fee for accommodations?” The first clause supports the 14-day answer. The available text says nothing about a fee, so the reply should explicitly leave that part unresolved. Use evidence IDs from the ingestion record for each supported claim.

Accept the request through FastAPI while stopping Redis temporarily. Verify the API records its receipt and the unsent outbox row. Restore Redis, observe the relay publish the row, and check that the worker starts from the pinned revision. Inspect the MCP result and confirm that neither the obsolete revision nor the other library's chunk enters the verifier request. Have the A2A peer reject an answer that cites an unrelated paragraph and require the coordinator to store a structured unresolved result after the allowed correction attempts. Repeat with a correct answer, kill a test worker after terminal commit but before acknowledging, and verify the next worker acknowledges without invoking the model again.

### Run it as a service

For local integration use Docker images with an unprivileged runtime user, pinned base and dependency versions, no build-time secrets in layers, and health checks that assert actual readiness. Compose can wire the test database, Redis, fixtures, and collector on an isolated network. Use separate database credentials for migrations, read-only policy queries, and task writers. Keep the verifier's identity limited to verification. Restrict network paths to the required cross-service destinations. Ensure telemetry omits article text, tokens, and credentials even when an exception is raised.

In Kubernetes, run the API and worker independently. Give the API a readiness condition for dependencies needed to accept a durable request. A broker outage can still allow intake if the outbox is available and queue age stays within policy. Worker readiness should mean it can consume work and commit state. Use liveness to detect an internally stuck service. Turning a downstream timeout into a liveness failure may restart every replica in a dependency outage. Put database migrations into a controlled job and change schemas compatibly before deployment. Use a safe migration order: add new fields, deploy readers and writers that tolerate both formats, backfill and verify, then retire old fields when all old workers are gone. For shutdown, stop claiming new work and allow active leases to finish within the grace period. Leave interrupted work recoverable.

Queue age and oldest outstanding task are better worker scaling signals than CPU alone when the workload spends most of its time awaiting services. Put a ceiling on concurrency at every downstream pool. For example, eight pods each configured for 16 in-flight tasks may generate more concurrent queries and tool calls than a 40-connection database pool can absorb. Design a normal-lane concurrency bound from the downstream budget and reserve some capacity for API health and recovery. Track cost per accepted and completed task, since retries that fail can still spend tokens.

### Establish measurable acceptance

| Area | Fixture or load | Passing evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data isolation | Two tenants, obsolete active-policy candidates, reused task IDs | Zero cross-tenant evidence IDs, and all citations point to the pinned current revision |
| Reliability | Kill a worker after a terminal update, pause Redis, repeat the same POST | One result for each accepted task, replay returns the same receipt, and pending work recovers within the documented recovery target |
| Quality | Known exact terms, paraphrases, and impossible questions | An example initial gate is recall at 5 of at least 0.90 on a 50-case judged fixture, zero unsupported claims on protected cases, and correct abstention for every deliberately unanswerable case |
| Latency | Ten minutes of representative synthetic traffic, including mixed prompt lengths | Example budget: intake p95 under 250 ms and end-to-end p95 under 15 s, with queue delay, provider delay, and error rate reported separately |
| Operability | Roll out a changed schema and revert a bad candidate with existing jobs in flight | Successful rollout and rollback, stable task IDs and result contracts, and dashboards and alerts that show the incident's cause |

Treat these numbers as proposed lab checks. Record fixture sizes, rate, duration, hardware, and dependency settings so another person can reproduce them. A good p95 during a test with many unmet or dropped requests is misleading. Count cancellations, terminal failures, and deadline misses in the denominator of the availability objective. Fail release for deterministic safety and data isolation failures before score-based evaluation. A language-model judge can help triage borderline evidence or clarity cases, but use human-calibrated rubrics and keep deterministic assertions for source membership, provenance, budget, and tool allowlists.
sections.debugging:
### The queue reports a task done but the API still says running

**Symptom:** The stream entry was acknowledged and no worker is active, while the task is still running in PostgreSQL.

**Root Cause:** The worker acknowledged the stream before committing the task's next durable transition. An exception, restart, or blocked database write left no delivery to drive recovery.

**Diagnostic:** Compare the task row's state, lease expiry and generation with the queue pending list and the attempt's recorded acknowledgement event. Look for an acknowledgement timestamp with no corresponding committed transition.

**Fix:** Acknowledge only after a terminal checkpoint or a durable retry handoff. Run reconciliation on expired nonterminal tasks and republish eligible work. Make the retry path idempotent so republishing does not reopen completed tasks.

### A correct policy is cited from the wrong branch

**Symptom:** Text is relevant and the answer sounds plausible, but the citation belongs to a different tenant or obsolete revision.

**Root Cause:** Cache keys use only the normalized question, or the last stage loads evidence without preserving the original tenant and revision filter.

**Diagnostic:** Inspect the rejected evidence ID, caller's tenant, pinned corpus revision, and resolved cache scope. Compare exact filtered search results to cached and approximate results for the same request. Use redacted identifiers rather than extracting the document into an incident log.

**Fix:** Scope every lookup and cache key by tenant, corpus revision, contract and search strategy version. Recheck scope when loading text and constructing verifier input. Add a test with the same question across two tenants and three revisions.

### Verification silently starts the same job more than once

**Symptom:** An A2A peer receives duplicate work whenever its initial response arrives late. Local latency and token use rise while the underlying answer stays the same.

**Root Cause:** The client treats a timeout as evidence that the peer never accepted the request. No durable correlation links the local delegation and remote task.

**Diagnostic:** Compare the task's recorded delegation operation, remote IDs, and attempt log. Look for several remote tasks with the same logical request. Identify which responses came after the client timeout.

**Fix:** Record a stable delegation identity before sending. Use a peer-supported correlation or idempotency contract, checkpoint the remote task ID when received, and resume it with status requests. Route cases with unknown outcomes to bounded reconciliation, then a terminal incomplete state if still unresolved.

### A rollout fails even though the new container answers health checks

**Symptom:** Newly accepted jobs complete, but tasks created before the rollout fail when workers deserialize their state.

**Root Cause:** The deployment introduced an incompatible job contract or database migration while old payloads remained in Redis and older workers still ran.

**Diagnostic:** Compare the contract version on failed tasks, worker image version, migrations and rollout order. Replay one old fixture through the candidate worker and one candidate fixture through the current reader in an isolated test.

**Fix:** Use additive schema changes and version contracts. Deploy tolerant consumers before new producers, drain or migrate incompatible work, and remove transitional fields only after measuring that old versions are gone.

### p95 latency increases even when the provider is healthy

**Symptom:** End-to-end latency rises while individual model call duration stays steady.

**Root Cause:** Work is accumulating before the model call. Retries, pool saturation, a blocked verifier, or queue starvation can shift delay into a different stage.

**Diagnostic:** Compare queue age, active tasks, rejected work, delay per stage, and the count of calls and retries per logical task. Check whether pooling and application-level concurrency exceed actual downstream capacity.

**Fix:** Reduce admission or protect a downstream with bounded concurrency and retry budgets. Scale the constrained worker group only when there is downstream headroom. End expired tasks instead of consuming resources to finish work that cannot meet its deadline.
sections.projects:
### Project 1: Knowledge Intake and Retrieval Platform

**Domain:** Public research

Deploy a full-stack search platform for research submissions. Support a review group submitting independent study summaries and later asking which evidence supports a claim. Include stable citation and correction history. Use synthetic submissions representing two independent research groups, including an explicit correction and a question for which no evidence exists.

#### Recommended Folder Structure

Create directories named apps/intake, apps/search, and packages/contracts. Add empty files named intake_api.py, evidence_search.py, and schemas.py. Create migrations, tests/retrieval, and operations directories with empty files named schema_plan.md, fixture_plan.md, and search_runbook.md.

#### Build Milestones

1. Define the monorepo, data services, retrieval pipeline, and typed tool boundary.
2. Evaluate retrieval, persistence, deployment readiness, and traceability end to end.

#### Acceptance Checklist

- Import and publish a corpus with subject labels and reviewer scopes. Replaying the same upload must return the existing record while a correction is published as a new revision. Document which states can be seen by each reviewer.
- Judge exact identifier lookups, paraphrases, unsupported claims, and withdrawn evidence. Record recall before and after fusion. Show that a query run by the wrong research group yields no restricted citations.
- Rebuild the embedding index from canonical submissions and verify documented citation behavior across revision changes. Prove that an interrupted rollout preserves accepted requests and that the operations runbook finds slow retrieval.

### Project 2: Service Coordination Platform

**Domain:** Facilities management

Coordinate independently deployable agents for maintenance requests. Use synthetic service tickets from two buildings. An intake service clarifies location and category. A peer scheduling service proposes windows. A human reviewer controls a simulated dispatch effect after seeing the specific destination, work order, and proposed time. No project uses real messaging or facility controls.

#### Recommended Folder Structure

Create apps/dispatch_api, apps/scheduling_peer, apps/work_worker, packages/contracts, and tests/failure. Add empty files named routes.py, scheduling.py, task_runner.py, approval_contract.py, and recovery_plan.md. Add a deploy directory with empty rollout_plan.md and an operations directory with empty on_call.md.

#### Build Milestones

1. Design MCP tools, A2A delegation, resumable queues, and approval for external effects.
2. Exercise failure recovery, task isolation, telemetry, and a safe rollout using synthetic requests.

#### Acceptance Checklist

- Give scheduling access only to the approved building and available windows. A cancellation during verification should prevent release of an effect. A peer response from an obsolete attempt should be recorded without changing the chosen slot.
- Simulate a lost acknowledgement, peer timeout, reissued dispatch notification, and approval expiry. Reconcile each case. Require fresh approval if the work order or recipient changes, and show the local simulated dispatch occurs once.
- Compare the previous and next contract versions in an integration run. Demonstrate rollback with jobs in flight and alert on backlog age rather than raw queue length alone.

### Project 3: Compliance Evidence Platform

**Domain:** Financial audit

Build a production-grade platform for evidence collection and review. Use fictional audit controls, file ownership, and retention deadlines. Given a control and period, gather read-only artifacts from permitted scopes and construct a candidate evidence package with provenance. A reviewer makes the actual disposition.

#### Recommended Folder Structure

Create apps/evidence_api, apps/validation_peer, and apps/review_worker with empty files named intake.py, verify_package.py, and review_states.py. Add packages/policy with an empty retention.py, tests/evals with an empty evaluation_matrix.md, and observability with empty service_objectives.md and incident_runbook.md files.

#### Build Milestones

1. Define data retention, security boundaries, evaluation gates, and operational dashboards.
2. Prove isolation, provenance, recovery, and performance against a recorded acceptance plan.

#### Acceptance Checklist

- Assert that separate audit teams cannot see one another's packages. Link each claim to an approved artifact version and reviewer decision. A missing artifact or expired evidence window must be clearly unresolved.
- Exercise deletion and retention across document, cache, evidence index, trajectory store, and backup policy. Record what a legal hold or active review changes. Keep operational dashboards free of identifiers and contents.
- Run isolated quality and performance gates for provenance, duplicate operations, time to package, and recovery from a worker loss. Redo the checks after upgrading a schema or model and run a rollout and rollback drill with an operator.
sections.quiz:
### Q1. A worker completes an external action but is terminated before updating its task record. What architecture minimizes duplicate effects?
- A. A larger model context
- B. Idempotency keys and persistent checkpoints with reconciliation
- C. Removing task states

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** A recoverable workflow needs durable coordination between the effect and its recorded state.

</details>

### Q2. Which evidence best supports a production readiness claim for the capstone?
- A. Passing end-to-end, failure-recovery, security, and evaluation checks linked to telemetry
- B. A diagram and one successful demonstration
- C. A large number of containers

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** Readiness includes behavior under failure, protection boundaries, operational visibility, and repeatable validation.

</details>

### Q3. A relay successfully publishes a Redis Stream entry and crashes before marking the outbox row sent. What should the system expect when the relay restarts?
- A. The outbox row is guaranteed to disappear
- B. Replaying the publication must use a new task ID
- C. Duplicate notifications are possible and workers must check durable task state
- D. PostgreSQL automatically removes the published Redis message

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: C.** Publication and marking sent cross a service boundary, so either step can succeed without the other. Keep the logical task ID stable and treat duplicate notifications as normal.

</details>

### Q4. An answer cites a semantically similar but superseded policy after the corpus is updated. What invariant prevents the issue?
- A. Rank all historical chunks together and ask the model to choose
- B. Require a pinned published revision in each search and citation lookup
- C. Raise the number of candidates returned by vector search
- D. Recreate the worker deployment on every policy edit

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: B.** Pinning gives a task a consistent evidence scope. Bound queries and caches by that scope, then validate citations against the approved revision before committing.

</details>

### Q5. A worker's lease expired during a slow model call. The new worker is already running the same task. Which update should the first worker make after its response arrives?
- A. Commit the answer because it started first
- B. Increase the expiration time and commit
- C. Write directly to the canonical answer and inform the new worker
- D. Try the conditional update and discard the stale result when the lease generation does not match

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: D.** A monotonically increasing lease generation fences obsolete attempts. Check the generation, status, and expiry in the transaction that writes the result.

</details>

### Q6. Which signal differentiates an overloaded queue from longer model calls when task p95 increases?
- A. Compare queue wait and model duration histograms, plus oldest queued task and completed count
- B. Inspect one provider latency sample
- C. Add task IDs as metric labels to retain detail
- D. Compare container image sizes between worker revisions

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

**Answer: A.** Per-stage histograms and the queue-age signal distinguish blocked work from slow execution. Individual task IDs belong in protected trace or log context, where they cannot create unbounded metric series.

</details>

### Q7. Short response. Describe what identity and task state an independently operated verifier needs to safely check a candidate answer and recover after a slow response.

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

The orchestrator selects an approved peer by configured identity and supported contract. It sends scoped evidence IDs or authorized excerpts with the candidate and a stable operation identity. The verifier checks its caller permissions and validates its answer schema. The orchestrator stores the remote task ID, polls bounded status, and accepts an artifact only if it belongs to the expected attempt, answer revision, and evidence set. Cancellation, deadlines, and unknown outcomes return explicit bounded states instead of spawning another untracked run.

</details>

### Q8. Short response. Propose one hard release gate, one measured quality gate, and one operability check for the library desk. Explain why they need different evidence.

<details>
<summary>Answer & Explanation</summary>

Require zero unauthorized evidence IDs on adversarial fixture cases as a deterministic safety gate. Measure recall at five and the supported-claim rate on a judged sample to characterize quality across exact names, paraphrases, and no-answer cases. Exercise a failed broker or killed worker in a staging rollout and prove the outbox and lease state recover. Trust-boundary assertions need binary checks, retrieval quality needs a representative denominator, and operability needs a real failure-and-recovery run with persisted state and telemetry.

</details>
sections.references:
### Review the deployment without leaving the lesson

Start the review with a small decisions record. For each component, write what it owns, what can be rebuilt, and how long recovery may take. A queue outage should exercise outbox lag and admission policy. A cache loss should cause extra source reads within connection budgets. A failed trajectory export should make investigation harder while task status still reflects the durable outcome. A disabled verifier should produce an explicit unverified or incomplete result. These distinctions prevent the same emergency “restart everything” procedure from being applied to failures with different ownership.

A high-quality capstone handoff contains a versioned corpus manifest, an agreed API and peer contract, a database recovery point, a scored fixture baseline, a dashboard export, and a drill log for redelivery, cancellation, and rollback. For each drill, record the simulated failure, the first visible symptom, the signal that identifies its cause, and the observed recovery time. Include one failure that leaves a task incomplete by design. Successful operation includes being able to explain which promises held and which could not be met.

Check retention across boundaries before signing off on the build. A pinned corpus revision gives reproducible citations, but a document may later be withdrawn or removed under policy. Define when stored results can still cite it, when they must be invalidated, and how you remove cache entries, index rows, and trajectory excerpts. Lost observability events can be tolerated in this lab. An untracked retained copy of withdrawn content cannot be treated as a harmless cache miss.

### Optional official documentation

- [FastAPI: deployment concepts](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/deployment/concepts/) — Read startup, replication, and memory use. Every server process has its own memory, so process-local task state cannot serve load-balanced clients after restart.
- [PostgreSQL: transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — Review Read Committed and concurrent updates. Use a uniqueness constraint and conditional writes for correctness rather than assuming an earlier read remains valid.
- [pgvector: filtering and approximate indexes](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#filtering) — Compare exact filtered search, iterative scans, and index strategies. Measure retrieval recall at real tenant selectivities before committing to an approximate index.
- [MCP specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) — Review server tools, schemas, and transports. Tool discovery advertises a capability. Invocation still requires authorization, validation, and time limits.
- [A2A documentation](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/) — Review Agent Cards, task state transitions, artifacts, and cancellation. Persist the remote identity and task handle to resume an independent verifier.
- [Kubernetes: Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) — Review rollout strategy and rollback. Pod readiness and schema compatibility are separate requirements that both need staging checks.
- [OpenTelemetry: observability primer](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/) — Use metrics to locate a system-wide problem, then use correlated traces and structured logs to inspect a particular execution.
